A lycanthrope is a human being who transforms — or is believed to transform — into a wolf. In plain terms, it is simply a more formal, scholarly word for a werewolf. The two words point to the same creature. "Werewolf" is casual and everyday; "lycanthrope" is the precise, technical term you'll find in serious writing, medical literature, or academic discussion.

The defining feature of a lycanthrope is the shift between two forms — human and wolf. A person walks in human skin by day, but becomes a beast, either partially or fully, under certain conditions. The most famous trigger is the full moon, though folklore varies: some traditions say the transformation is caused by a curse, a bite from another lycanthrope, a deal with dark forces, or a magic ritual.

This is an important distinction. In some traditions, a lycanthrope has no control over the change — the full moon forces it upon them, often against their will, like a sickness they cannot escape. In others, the lycanthrope can choose when to transform, making it a power rather than a curse. Modern fiction tends to explore both angles, sometimes even within the same story.
What a lycanthrope is like in wolf form

Across most folklore and fiction, a lycanthrope in wolf form is not simply a regular wolf. It is something more dangerous — retaining human cunning while gaining animal ferocity. Common traits include:

  • Superhuman strength and speed
  • Heightened senses (smell, hearing, sight)
  • Near-inability to feel pain
  • Loss of moral inhibition — they may kill, hunt, or destroy without the conscience that governs them in human form

When they return to human form, they often remember nothing of what they did. This makes the lycanthrope a tragic figure in many stories — a person who wakes up to discover what they've done with no memory of doing it.

In widespread European folklore and most of its fictional descendants, a lycanthrope cannot be killed by ordinary means — bullets, blades, and blows that would kill a human simply heal too fast. The one reliable exception is silver, which disrupts their supernatural nature. A silver bullet or silver blade is the classic way to kill a lycanthrope.

The person is a lycanthrope. The condition itself — the curse, disorder, or supernatural affliction — is called lycanthropy. So you might say: "He was a lycanthrope, suffering from lycanthropy since the night of the attack."

The word has a second, real-world use in psychiatry. Clinical lycanthropy is a documented (though extremely rare) mental condition in which a person sincerely believes they are physically transforming into an animal — most often a wolf. They don't actually change; it is a delusion. But the experience feels completely real to them. So in a medical context, calling someone a "lycanthrope" means they suffer from this delusional disorder, not that they are literally a monster from folklore.

Strictly speaking, lycanthrope means wolf-transformation. But in fantasy literature and games, the word is sometimes used more loosely to include people who transform into any large predatory animal — bears, tigers, lions, etc. These are sometimes called therianthropes (the broader term for any human-animal shapeshifter), but writers often use "lycanthrope" as a catch-all. When in doubt, context will tell you whether the author means wolf specifically or shapeshifters generally.

A lycanthrope is a person who transforms into a wolf — a werewolf, in everyday language. The transformation may be forced (by the moon or a curse) or willed (as a dark power). In wolf form, the lycanthrope is stronger, faster, and more dangerous than any natural animal, but often loses memory and moral control. Silver is their weakness. In medicine, the word refers to a rare delusion where someone believes they are transforming. The related word "lycanthropy" names the condition itself.
